quests.hint: A plan of times for events. It opens with the same three letters as 'school', in any accent.
quests.explanation: Sch-ed-ule opens with sch, and the ending is -ule, said /juːl/. The British /ʃ/ and American /sk/ pronunciations use the same spelling.

quests.hint: A person you work with. The ending is -gue, and the u is silent.
quests.explanation: Col-league has -ague, in which the ea says /iː/ and the u only keeps the g hard. The word league sits inside it.

quests.hint: Scattered broken pieces left after something is destroyed. It is a French word, and its last letter is silent.
quests.explanation: De-bris keeps its French spelling, so the final s is not pronounced. French loans often keep a silent last consonant: debris, chassis, corps.

quests.hint: From another country. It has ei, and the g is silent.
quests.explanation: For-eign belongs to a small -eign group with reign and sovereign, in which the g is not pronounced. The ei is not the usual /iː/.

quests.hint: Free time. It has ei, and the middle sound is /ʒ/.
quests.explanation: Lei-sure breaks the 'i before e' rhyme, and the -sure says /ʒə/, as in measure. The first vowel varies by accent, but the spelling stays.

quests.hint: Very old. The /ʃ/ sound is written with c and i.
quests.explanation: An-cient has ci for /ʃ/, like special, and it ends in -ent. The e comes after i, unlike receive, where ei follows c.

quests.hint: A source you mention, or someone who vouches for you. Unlike 'referred', it does not double.
quests.explanation: Refer + ence: the stress moves to the first syllable (REF-er-ence), so the r stays single. The doubling happens only when the last syllable is stressed.

quests.hint: Keeping something in working order. It comes from 'maintain', but its vowels shift.
quests.explanation: Maintain becomes maintenance: the ai turns into e, giving main-te-nance. Writing 'maintainance' keeps the ai from maintain, which the noun gives up.

quests.hint: A place where someone lives. Its verb is 'reside', but the noun ends differently.
quests.explanation: Reside loses its e before -ence: residence. The c makes /s/, and the same -ence appears in resident.

quests.hint: An official paper that proves something. It has four syllables and ends in -ate.
quests.explanation: Cer-tif-i-cate comes from the verb certify. The -fy of the verb becomes -fic before -ate, and the noun ends in -icate.

quests.hint: Money awarded to help someone study. The opening /sk/ is written sch.
quests.explanation: Scholar + ship: -ar stays, and -ship marks a status, as in friendship. The sch- says /sk/, as in the word school.

quests.hint: A talk given to students. The /tʃ/ sound is written ture after a c.
quests.explanation: Lec-ture: the c says /k/ and -ture says /tʃə/. The same -ture ending is in picture and culture.

quests.hint: A person who works for a company. It ends in a stressed /iː/.
quests.explanation: Em-ploy-ee: the -ee names the person affected by an action, as in trainee and referee. The y of employ stays as it is.

quests.hint: A formal conversation for a job. It is built from a prefix meaning 'between' and a word for seeing.
quests.explanation: Inter + view: the prefix has one t and one r, and nothing is changed. It is not 'enterview'.

quests.hint: A form you submit. It comes from the verb 'apply'; think about what happens to its y.
quests.explanation: Apply changes its y to i before -cation: application. The double p comes from the prefix ap- before the base.

quests.hint: Honestly, or a way to end a formal letter. The base ends in e.
quests.explanation: Sincere + ly keeps the e, because -ly begins with a consonant. The same idea worked in 'lovely'.

quests.hint: A file sent with an email. The verb behind it starts with a double letter.
quests.explanation: At-tach + ment: the tt comes from the prefix meeting the base, and -ment goes on without change. The tempting wrong form is 'attachement'.

quests.hint: A single item in a recipe. The ending has ie, said /iənt/.
quests.explanation: In-gre-di-ent has ie because the i belongs to the Latin root (ingredi, to go in), not because of the 'i before e' rhyme. The ending is -ent.

quests.hint: The study of the mind. It opens with a silent letter.
quests.explanation: Psy-chol-o-gy has a silent p, and ch says /k/. Both come from Greek: psyche (mind) and logos (study).

quests.hint: An organised effort, such as a political one. It ends with a silent g.
quests.explanation: Cam-paign ends in -aign, said /eɪn/. The g is silent, as in sign and foreign.

quests.hint: Extremely tired. A letter after the x is written but not spoken.
quests.explanation: Ex-haust-ed has a silent h after x, and -au- says /ɔː/. The word is spelled as ex + haust, not 'exausted'.

quests.hint: Being alive or real. The verb behind it is 'exist'.
quests.explanation: Exist + ence: the noun ends in -ence, not -ance. Watch out for the slip 'existance'.

quests.hint: Doing a task, or a show on stage. The verb behind it is 'perform'.
quests.explanation: Perform + ance keeps every letter of the base and ends in -ance, so it is not 'performence'.

quests.hint: Ease or handiness. Two vowels sit together before -ence.
quests.explanation: Con-ven-ience has ie before -ence, as in the adjective convenient. The spelling 'conveniance' looks plausible but is wrong.

quests.hint: To provide space, or to adapt to someone's needs. It has two doubled letters.
quests.explanation: Ac-com-mo-date has cc and mm. It ends in -ate. It is one of the most frequently misspelled words in English.

quests.hint: Lines that run side by side and never meet. There is a famous trick hidden in the middle.
quests.explanation: Par-al-lel has ll in the middle, and the two l's look like parallel lines. The last l is single, and the word is not 'paralel'.

quests.hint: A period of one thousand years. It has two doubled letters, and one comes from the word for 'year'.
quests.explanation: Mil-len-ni-um joins Latin mille (thousand) and annus (year). The nn comes from annus, and the ll from mille.

quests.hint: Playfully naughty. It has three syllables, though many people add a fourth.
quests.explanation: Mis-chie-vous ends in -ievous, not -ious with an extra i. Adding an extra i gives 'mischievious', which is wrong.

quests.hint: A person who moves permanently to another country. Its prefix meets a base that begins with m.
quests.explanation: Im + migrant: the prefix in- becomes im- before m, giving a double m, as in immediately. Emigrant, someone who leaves, has a single m after e-.

quests.hint: Giving something up for a greater goal. The last syllable sounds like /fɪs/ but is not written that way.
quests.explanation: Sac-ri-fice ends in -fice, said /fɪs/, as in office. It joins Latin sacer (holy) and facere (to make), and the ending keeps the Latin spelling.
